slides.text:
Big tools are split into **subcommands**: `git commit`, `docker run`, `go build`. Each one does one job, and each has its own code.

In cobra, the root command is the tool and every subcommand hangs from it, like a tree. The sketch below is not Go.
slides.code:
app
├── greet           app greet
└── config          app config
    └── set         app config set

slides.text:
Two sessions:

- **Session 1:** create a subcommand, attach it to the root and read its name
- **Session 2:** subcommands inside subcommands, deeper trees and listing the children of a command
A subcommand is a `*cobra.Command`, built the same way as the root: it has its own `Use` and its own `Run`.

A command does not become a subcommand by existing. You must attach it with `AddCommand`, on the command that will be its parent.

Only the first word of `Use` is the name you type. The rest is usage text.

exercises.title: What does `app` run?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what runs when you type `app` alone.
exercises.explanation: With no subcommand typed, cobra runs the root's own `Run`. The help appears only when the root has no `Run`.

slides.text: Any command can hold subcommands, not only the root. A command that only groups others usually has no `Run`: when you run it alone, cobra shows its help.

Every command knows its parent, so `CommandPath` joins the names from the root down, however deep the tree is. `Commands()` goes the other way: it returns the subcommands a command holds, sorted by name.
